items.snippet: Funding the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout began with cash—over $700 bill...
items.raw_snippet:
Funding the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout began with cash—over $700 billion sitting on the balance sheets of the biggest tech companies in the world. Then came private capital, with alternative investors expected to supply $1.4 trillion over the next five years, followed by a wave of public corporate debt issuance to the tune of $2.1 trillion of expected AI-related debt financing over the same period. Now, the next level of financing is moving into one of the most traditional venues: [...] Companies in the United States are on track to raise around $290 billion in 2026 through just IPOs, approaching the 2021 peak of roughly $330 billion.1 That marks one of the strongest years of issuance in the last two decades before accounting for secondary offerings, special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs) or convertible notes. But just as the AI buildout grows, so do the capital markets. It’s a large amount, but in the context of today’s $70 trillion stock market, expected issuance [...] IPOs with a $100 billion raise and $2 trillion valuation have been estimated to have a 1%–1.2% weight in the NASDAQ 100 and S&P Total Market Index.2 In the MSCI World Indexes, large IPOs can amount to a weight of roughly 10–11 basis points and be considered for early inclusion as soon as the 10th trading day.

Even with a pipeline of private companies ultimately debuting in the public markets, the case to stay private for longer still holds. It’s the role of public markets that’s changing.

items.raw_snippet: No surprise: AI has the highest valuations. Aventis Advisors puts the median revenue multiple in a sample of recent large AI funding rounds and acquisitions at 24.2 times, with the highest individual transaction at 225 times. Aventis cautions that the sample skews toward the largest, most successful companies, “so founders looking to sell their AI startups should take this data with a grain of salt. The valuation multiple will likely be significantly lower in the sale offer you receive.” [...] Investors and acquirers also place more weight on profit than revenue growth when valuing IT services startups, although the absolute size of the business matters a lot, too. An Aventis analysis of M&A transactions of IT services businesses from 2015 to mid-2026 notes a median EV/EBITDA multiple of 10.4 times for the period, with a peak of 12.7 times in 2023 and a low of 8.5 times in 2020. The median for 2025 was 9.5 times. AI is dividing this category, too. Data analytics, cybersecurity, and [...] Two startups with the same $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR) can walk out of a fundraising round with very different valuations. That’s because there is no single tech startup valuation multiple in 2026. Investors now price AI-native companies and traditional software-as-a-service (SaaS) businesses as separate markets, and a startup gets the multiple of whichever market investors decide it’s in. items.snippet: Title: P1 Guest Talk by Yvonne Rogers | Event | Pioneer Centre for Artificial In...
items.raw_snippet:
Title: P1 Guest Talk by Yvonne Rogers | Event | Pioneer Centre for Artificial Intelligence
Out of Our Minds: What is AI Doing to Us and for Us? The phrase ‘out of our minds’ refers to how we externalise and offload various aspects of cognitive work through writing, drawing, talking and so on. AI is the latest technological tool that we use to do this. This can result in a paradox of effort where the extent to which we externalise is reduced leading to less satisfaction. Simply put, when we make the effort ourselves to perform a task it can be more rewarding than when we get AI to do it for us. How can we design AI tools to make our work more effortful (rather than less) and in doing so more rewarding? In my talk, I will describe the research I have been doing investigating how best to extend human minds that can be both rewarding and challenging: enabling us to reason and make decisions more systematically through reflecting on our goals and intent. **Yvonne Rogers** is a Professor of Interaction Design at UCL. From 2022-2024 she was the CTO of LetsThink.com, a start-up that is developing new tools to augment how people think by applying behaviour science methods to AI. During this time, she co-developed a centre for AI and healthcare, that focussed on how personal health data could be used in combination with AI from a human-centred perspective to improve health and well-being. In 2022, she was awarded the ACM SIGCHI Lifetime Research Award; the Royal Society Robin Milner Medal for Computer Science and was elected as a Fellow of the Royal Society as "one of the leaders who created the field of Ubiquitous Computing". She also received a MRC Suffrage and Science Award (2020) for being one of the leading women in 'mathematics and computing.' She is also a Fellow of the ACM; a Fellow of the British Computer Society and a Fellow of the ACM's CHI Academy. ***After the talk, we invite you to join us for a reception at 16.00-17.00 in the Seminar Room at the Pioneer Centre for AI, Øster Voldgade 3, 1350 Kbh K.***.
